name: crema mexicana
instructions:
Rick Bayless's two homemade mexican-style cremas — cultured heavy cream in the crema de rancho tradition. VERSION 1 (buttermilk-cultured) is luscious, nutty, and most like real crema de rancho, but finicky and melts quickly on warm food. VERSION 2 (sour-cream-cultured) is more sour but more foolproof and stays stable spooned onto warm flautas and such.

=== VERSION 1 — BUTTERMILK CULTURE (NUTTY, CREMA-DE-RANCHO-LIKE, FINICKY) ===

INGREDIENTS:
- 2 cups heavy/whipping cream (best flavor = NOT ultrapasteurized)
- 1/2 cup buttermilk (do your best to confirm it contains LIVE CULTURES)
- 2 tbsp powdered milk (not essential, but gives a richer texture)

PROCEDURE:
1. WARM the cream to about 80-90°F — no warmer than body temperature. Pour into a very clean 3-4 cup container with a tight-fitting lid.
2. BLEND the buttermilk and milk powder (blender or immersion blender) until no traces of powder remain.
3. STIR the buttermilk mixture into the cream. COVER LIGHTLY — if the lid screws or snaps on, DON'T SEAL IT.
4. CULTURE in a draft-free warmish place (80-90°F if available) until noticeably thicker, 6-12 hours (longer if the space is cool).
5. REFRIGERATE 6+ hours to fully thicken.

=== VERSION 2 — SOUR CREAM CULTURE (MORE SOUR, FOOLPROOF, HEAT-STABLE) ===

INGREDIENTS:
- 2 cups heavy/whipping cream (NOT ultrapasteurized)
- 1/2 cup best-quality sour cream (live cultures)

PROCEDURE:
1. WARM the cream to 80-90°F, pour into a very clean lidded container.
2. WHISK in the sour cream. Cover lightly (don't seal).
3. CULTURE 6-12 hours in a draft-free warmish place until noticeably thicker.
4. REFRIGERATE 6+ hours to fully thicken.

=== STORAGE ===

Both versions keep, covered, SEVERAL WEEKS in the refrigerator.
notes:
=== SOURCE + WHAT REAL CREMA IS ===

Rick Bayless. The target is CREMA DE RANCHO — cultured heavy cream straight from the ranch (his touchstones: the dairy vendors at Mercado de San Juan and Mercado Medellín in Mexico City). CRÈME FRAÎCHE is the closest store-bought substitute. Most tubs labeled 'mexican crema' on either side of the border are one of two fakes: (1) half-and-half richness + gums, no live-culture nuttiness/sourness at all, or (2) half-and-half richness + gums + souring culture — essentially american sour cream, just creamier and a little less thick.

=== WHICH VERSION TO MAKE ===

- VERSION 1 (buttermilk): luscious, nutty, most like crema de rancho — but finicky, and it MELTS QUICKLY spooned on anything warm.
- VERSION 2 (sour cream): more sour, but foolproof and STABLE ON WARM FOOD (flautas etc.).

=== THE LAZY SHORTCUT — NAIVE MIX, NO CULTURE ===

Just mixing sour cream and heavy cream naively (no warming, no culturing wait) WORKS IN A PINCH — better than no crema.

=== DAIRY VARIABILITY — AND THE FAILURE FALLBACK ===

Bayless's caveat: dairy is variable (breed, feed, season, pasteurization/homogenization, which cultures and whether they're still alive), so results vary. If your cultured cream doesn't come out perfectly, USE IT IN A SAUCE OR DESSERT where heavy cream (not whipped cream) would be welcome — it's not wasted.

=== WHY LEAVING IT OUT IS SAFE — THE CULTURES OUTRUN SPOILAGE ===

Isn't this just two perishable dairy products left on the counter? No — it's the yogurt/crème fraîche move. Pasteurized cream starts nearly sterile; the live-culture inoculant (sour cream or buttermilk) floods it with lactic acid bacteria that bloom at 80-90°F and acidify the cream before anything else can get a foothold. The thickening you're watching for IS the acidification — by the time it's noticeably thicker, it has preserved itself (hence the weeks of fridge life). This is why the fine print is load-bearing: LIVE cultures, a VERY CLEAN container, no warmer than body temperature.

THE FAILURE TELL: if it never thickens in the window, the culturing failed and it really has just been cream sitting warm — that's when the cooked-sauce fallback (or the trash) applies. Gas bubbles, mold, or a yeasty/bitter smell = toss.

=== KEY TECHNIQUE POINTS ===

- NOT ultrapasteurized cream — flavor and culturing both suffer.
- No warmer than BODY TEMPERATURE when warming the cream (80-90°F).
- Lid on LIGHTLY, never sealed, during the culture.
- The powdered milk in version 1 is optional but buys a richer texture.
